en: The *Kālacakrāvatāra* by the venerable scholar Abhayākaragupta. Oṃ! Homage to Mañjuśrī!

I bow to my own Jina, who is for all people, who possesses a body that is formless yet composed of forms and other qualities, whose nature is beyond conceptual construction, and who bears a universal form characterized by infinite tranquility through the non-duality of wisdom and compassion.
Those luminaries which once bestowed beauty upon the sky and announced both prosperity and calamity,
now, as if having entered the interior of the earth, they are overcome by darkness.

For here, indeed, because the heterodox teachers (tīrthika), afflicted by stinginess, have concealed the established astronomical system (siddhānta) even though they composed a simplified calculation (laghukaraṇa) with many elaborations, it is not understood nowadays; therefore, that [system] is now set forth.
One should write four hundred and three [years];
when a year begins from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, then it must be combined with this [correction].
That [number], diminished by one hundred and eighty-two, becomes the pure annual constant (*varṣadhruvaka*). That, multiplied by the elapsed days, is the lunar-day aggregate (*māsapiṇḍa*),
occurring within the months beginning with Caitra, from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon.

That [sum] mixed with those [values] is placed in two positions; the lower one is multiplied by four, divided by zero-three-one (130), and when the remainder of the division is dropped and the quotient is added to the upper position, the pure lunar-month total (*māsapiṇḍa*) results. However, when there is a double year, then a year must be treated as thirteen months, and one month should be counted for each [double] year.
And the entry into the month of Caitra must not be performed.
Having placed that pure monthly total in three places, it is multiplied by eleven (kara-śikhin). From the middle value, one-sixth of the lower value is to be subtracted;
if there is a remainder of the division, from that as well, one-sixth of the quotient is to be subtracted.
Here, from the lower value increased by thirty, the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty should be added to the upper value increased by two;
the remainder of the division shall be the *daṇḍapiṇḍa*.
The remainder of the upper value divided by seven shall be the *vārapiṇḍa*.
But nothing is obtained.

Again, having placed the pure month-pile (māsapiṇḍa) mixed with one hundred and twelve in two places, the remainder from the division by six in the lower position shall be the component of the pile. The quotient obtained from the division, increased by five, should be added to the head after being multiplied by two; this is the *Kālacakra-avatāra*.
Then, from the remainder of the division by twenty-eight from the *mūrdhva* [value], the *padapiṇḍa* (cluster of feet) shall be obtained.
Here, the sequence of the *vārapiṇḍa*, *daṇḍapiṇḍa*, *padapiṇḍa*, and the parts of the *piṇḍa* should be written down one below the other.

Again, the pure months situated in the three places, multiplied by the lords of the middle position, should be divided by forty-nine; the quotient added to two, and then divided by sixty *ghaṭīs*, with the remainder of the division being known as the *nakṣatra-ghaṭīs*.
The quotient obtained when [the total] is divided by two is the *mūrdhan* (head).
Then, the remainder from dividing that *mūrdhan* by twenty-seven is to be known as the *nakṣatra-piṇḍa* (stellar aggregate).
Here, below the *ṛtyu-piṇḍa*, the *ṛtyu-ghaṭī-piṇḍa* (aggregate of death-hours) should be written.

When neither the year nor the month is entered into the year-heap (*varṣarāśi*) and the pure-month heap (*śuddhamāsapiṇḍa*), then, in each month, one, thirty-two, two, and one should be added respectively to the components of the weekday, *daṇḍa*, *pada*, and the heap; furthermore, two and eleven should be added to the minutes (*ghaṭī*).
At the commencement of the year and so forth, a different set of weekdays, heaps, and so on must be calculated.
The purpose [of the calculation] is for the daily weekday (*vāra*) and for the duration of the lunar day (*tithi*).

For the duration of the lunar day, the elapsed and current lunar days of the current month, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), are to be added or subtracted, or added again, respectively, into the weekday, *nāḍī*, and *pada* positions.
When two [units] are obtained as the quotient of dividing the *piṇḍa* by fourteen, the fourth part of those two, or the *piṇḍa* itself if it is even, is to be added.
When one or three [units] are obtained, it is uneven;
there is no further division beyond this,
because no more aggregates (piṇḍa) are obtainable above twenty-seven.

[This is] by way of twenty-eight parts. Therefore, when combined with thirty lunar days (*tithis*), they do not exceed fifty-seven. When the remainder of the division is even, the lunar steps (*candrapada*) are to be added; when odd, they are to be subtracted. Regarding the zero remainder: zero is purified in the case of the lunar step of the thirty-three (*tridaśaśaśipada*); in the case of the five-eyes and sun (*pañcanetrārka*), it is ten; in the case of the lunar day (*tithi*)—the eleventh—it is fire (*agni*); in the case of the ten-ocean step, it is twenty minus one; in the case of the twenty-two and five-hollows (*pañcarandhra*), it is seasons (*ṛtu*) and Vasu (*vasu*); in the seventh, it is twenty-five. In that [case], all [values] are to be added or subtracted according to the divisions of the signs (*rāśi*) as manifested by the sun.
"In the pure" means that there is nothing whatsoever to be given or to be abandoned. "In that" refers to the mass of the water-clock (ghaṭīpiṇḍa).
By the differentiation of the sun, there arise the solar positions.
The debt of the sun is a debt in that [reckoning], and the wealth of the sun is wealth in that; this is the distinction regarding the sun.

This is stated in the *Kālacakrāvatāra*: "By the method to be explained, having either added or subtracted the quotient obtained from the division by the elements (five) and so forth, the days of the week and the steps of movement are combined; this is called the 'sun' (*ravi*). If it is to be added to the solar longitude, then it is to be added to the wheel of the days of the week."
Now, that which is to be added is for the solar enjoyment (*sūryabhoga*), and that which is to be subtracted is for the lunar.

These two alone constitute the pure solar [values] for the moon; these are the lunar positions (*candrapadāni*) in the sequence of elements (*bhūta-bhūteṣu*): four, three, and one, in the eastern part and likewise in the other.

In the eastern part, having drawn a horizontal line in the middle according to the upward lunar sequence, in the other [part], one should write below according to the downward sequence starting from the moon; thus there are fourteen. In this way, all [the values] consist of *ghaṭikās*.
In this case, the remainder of the fourteen parts constitutes the first step of the movement; the one above that is the subsequent movement.
A planet has entered therein.
Having multiplied the components of the aggregate by that [remainder], one obtains the result through division by one hundred and twenty-six.
The first half is the "eaten" (bhukta) position;
having discarded that by means of the second half, or rather, the "uneaten" (abhukta) position itself should be added to or subtracted from the place of the ghatis of the weekday.

This is what is said: having mixed the result obtained from the division by the elapsed [periods] and so forth according to the method to be described, and having discarded it, however many combined solar steps (ravicaraṇapada) there may be, that much—called the "sun-portion" (ravikā)—should be added to the solar longitude (sūryabhoga).
Then it should be added to the weekday-line;
if it is to be subtracted from the solar longitude,
then it should be subtracted from this [weekday-line].

The two [cycles] of the Moon are the pure Sun-cycle and the Moon-Sun-cycle; these are the lunar positions among the elements (bhūta) and non-elements (abhūta). Regarding the Fire-ray-Moon [cycle], in the eastern and western portions, one should write them in the eastern portion in ascending order from above, placing a horizontal line in the middle, and in the western portion in reverse order starting from the Moon and so on; thus there are fourteen, all of which consist of the ghaṭikās of the planetary transits (prahāṇa).
Here, the position of transit established by the remainder of the fourteen parts is the transit above that.
Therein, the planet has entered [the sign].
Having multiplied the portion of the [current] segment by that [multiplier], one obtains the quotient by means of a divisor of one hundred and twenty-six;
this is the elapsed portion and the position in the first half.
In the latter half [of the calculation], however, having discarded that [result], it should be added to or subtracted from the position of the ghaṭikās of the weekday, or else left as it is.

Why? Because the solar units (ravikā) here are impure; therefore, for the sake of obtaining pure solar units, one adds one or more units to the weekday position to indicate the day of the week, starting with Sunday (Āditya).

The *daṇḍas* and so forth for a lunar day (*tithi*) are to be consumed starting from sunrise. For the purpose of calculating the Sun’s transit through a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) each day, the lunar day stated as beginning with the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) is placed in two locations; in one it is multiplied by four *daṇḍas*, and in the other, according to the method of the *Karaṇas*, it is [multiplied] by twenty or twenty-two *pāṇīpala*s, following the system of the *Kālacakra-avatāra*.

Alternatively, by means of the Siddhānta placement, having divided by twenty-six *pāṇīpalas* and then divided by sixty, one should add the quotient to the upper [place]. Having also divided the upper *daṇḍas* by sixty, the quotient should be added to the asterism (*ṛkṣa*). The remainder of the division is the *daṇḍas* of the asterism; one should write the *pāṇīpalas* below the *daṇḍas* of the asterism. When the asterism, its *daṇḍas*, the aggregate of *pāṇīpalas*, and the *pāṇīpalas* have been placed in two locations, one should subtract six asterisms from the three-quarter [position] in one place for the sake of the sun's [longitude].
The sign [of the moon] subtracted from Aries, Aśvinī, and so forth, shall be the next sign as the birth-sign (janmarāśi).
It is said:
"In Aries, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, [the lords are] the Moon, Venus, and the Sun."
Mars, the minister (Saturn), Rāhu, Mercury, and the one who bears the fruit of Śani (Jupiter) are situated in Sagittarius at its beginning and end, starting from Scorpio.
Regarding the phrase "beginning and end":
Saturn is at the beginning of the bow (cāpa) and Ketu is at its end.

In this case, if the debt (ṛṇa) is greater than the [remaining] portion of the zodiacal sign, then it should be subtracted after adding twenty-seven to the position of the asterism (ṛkṣa) within the circle of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatra-cakra).
If the remainder after subtraction should be half a circle,
then that half-circle is to be subtracted;
at that very point, it should be understood as being in reverse order (utkrama).
If the half-circle has not been subtracted, the sequence remains as it is.

From the asterism divided by sixty, one should add the minutes situated below; the quotient obtained by dividing by fifteen (five elements and three fires) indicates the planetary position in the quarters of the zodiac signs. Having identified that planetary position in the quarters of the signs, one should discard [the remainder]. In the calculation of the slow motion (*mandakārya*), there are six sign-quarters for the Moon, while in the case of birth signs beginning with Cancer (*karka*), there are five.

There are exactly this many *pada*s for the slow-motion (*mandakārya*) of all planets; these are the *bhāga*s starting from Earth (1) and so forth. However, when a remainder is obtained, it should be understood that the planet stands in the first *pada* in every case.
Then, the operation to be performed—“divided by that” and so forth—is as will be stated hereafter.
At that time, in the slow-motion of all planets, [the result] should be known as a debt (*ṛṇa*) in direct order (*krama*) and a credit (*dhana*) in reverse order (*utkrama*).
Then, from the portion already traversed, a second portion is to be traversed.

From the *nāḍīs* remaining after being divided by that [portion], the degrees traversed by the planet—calculated according to the first half of the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) together with the traversed portion of the *bhūtādi* division—are aggregated. However, in the latter half, having subtracted the traversed portion obtained by division, the untraversed portions of the degrees are aggregated along with the other traversed portion; these are to be added to or subtracted from the planetary *nāḍīs* according to whether they are positive or negative. This very result is the "pure sun" (*śuddharavikā*) for the Sun.

The *Kālacakrāvatāra*: regarding the sun, the asterism and so forth that have been traversed in the place of the asterisms are the "consumed" (*bhukta*); the remainder of what has been consumed is the "to-be-consumed" (*bhoktavya*).
This is likewise for the moon and the yoga to be explained hereafter.
Here, in Cancer and the following signs, the time [of death] is within a fortnight.
In the second half of Cancer, the value is six (rasa).
In this manner, it continues until Sagittarius, where the value is three (vahni) and zero (kha) at the end of the solstice; likewise, from Capricorn onwards, the value is negative (dhanam).

For the purpose of calculating the Moon’s transit through the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the lunar days (tithis) stated for the bright fortnight and so forth should be added to the position of the Sun in the nakṣatra column.
Thereafter, those lunar days (tithis), multiplied by six (rasa) and added to the elapsed ghaṭīs and so forth of the weekday, constitute the solar debt in ghaṭīs;
this should be understood as a subtraction from the ghaṭī-place.
From this, the lunar motion (candrabhoga) shall result.
The lunar day (tithi) is derived from the difference between the solar and lunar longitudes.
When the lunar days stated for the beginning of the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) are doubled and reduced by one, the remainder after division by seven—wherever possible—is the *karaṇa*.
The *karaṇa* is the same as the duration of the lunar day (*tithi-bhoga*).
In this regard, the general rule is as follows:
those breaths which do not remain above the location of the breath enter into the *pāṇīpala*s by means of the quotient obtained through division by six.
Those [remaining units] also persist for half of sixty.
The quotient obtained by dividing by sixty enters into the *ghaṭīs*.
The *ghaṭīs* likewise enter into the weekday or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Even the days of the week (*vāra*) perish after becoming seven;
likewise, even the twenty-seven constellations (*nakṣatra*) do not remain here once they have come into being?
The same applies to the *yogas*: thus, one constellation consists of sixty *daṇḍas*, as do a *yoga* and a day.
In that regard, the *vāras* (days of the week) are seven, beginning with Āditya and the others.
The *tithis* (lunar days) are fifteen, beginning with the first day (*pratipad*).

The *nakṣatras* (lunar mansions) are twenty-seven: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Raivatī.

Likewise, there are twenty-seven yogas: Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Kālacakrāvatāra, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, Śiva, Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti.
The *karaṇas* are seven: Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Garaja, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi;
likewise, there are eleven others: Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna as the eleventh.

Among these, starting from the latter half of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), each has an enjoyment (*bhoga*) of four *praharas* respectively; by repeating this sequence again and again, the enjoyment of the seven [initial ones] continues until the first half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī*).

From the latter half of that [tithi] until the first half of the first day (śukla-pratipad) of the following month, the enjoyment of the other four lunar days (tithis) should be understood by dividing them into two equal parts, establishing the distinction between their former and latter halves; such is the sequence of the fivefold calendar (pañcāṅga) consisting of the day of the week, lunar day, asterism, yoga, and karaṇa.
Aries consists of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and one quarter of Kṛttikā;

in this manner, by means of nine quarters each, the twelve zodiac signs—Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—are to be known as corresponding to the months beginning with Vaiśākha. Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, and Sun; Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn, and Jupiter are considered the presiding deities of these signs respectively. As for the positions of the planets within these signs: [the sequence follows].

The pure years (śuddhavarṣāṇi) are the pure years (śuddhābdāḥ) increased by eight; these are multiplied by four hundred and separately diminished by the pure years increased by eight. The resulting quotient from division by one hundred and seventeen is added to two to obtain the days of the week. From the remainders of that division, multiplied by sixty and converted into nāḍīs, the quotient obtained by division by seven is to be taken, and the remainder of the division is to be discarded.
To the obtained *ghaṭīs*, thirty are added; the result is divided by sixty, and two are added to the quotient.
The remainder of this division is the *vāra-ghaṭikā* (the weekday-hour constant), which is placed below.
Furthermore, the remainder from dividing the weekdays by seven is the *varṣa-saṃkrānti-vāra-dhruvaka* (the weekday constant for the solar ingress of the year), which should be placed above.

In this context, when the sun leaves Pisces and enters Aries, twelve are subtracted; these are the subtrahends (*kṣepaka*) for Aries and the subsequent signs in their respective order: one, seven, twenty-five, four, three, five, thirty-one, sixteen, and twenty-three in the third [sign].
In the sixth [house], the Moon becomes the fire of the Vedas; with a pair of eyes and hands, there are twenty-four [years].

The *Kālacakrāvatāra* states: "Six moons, five and one moon, mountain, pair, fire; six moons, Vedas, mountains, worlds; six Vedas, zero-zero; and the position of two eyes and five arrows for the Sun in the sign of Pisces."
This is their placement (*nyāsa*).

Among these, for each of the twelve compartments, the first [value] is to be given as the weekday constant (*vāradhruva*), and the second is the *ghaṭī* constant beginning with fifty-seven (*saptapañcāśad-ādika*). Thus, the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) and its duration in days and *ghaṭīs* are to be known from the *karaṇa*. Now, the calculation of days (*ahan-gaṇa*) is stated for the purpose of determining the duration of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-bhoga*) starting from Mars (*maṅgala*).

The pure months, multiplied by thirty for the purpose of the heap of days, are added to the lunar dates (tithis) stated for the bright fortnight and so forth; having placed these in three positions, one should divide the lower heap by 703 (seven hundred and three). The quotient obtained should be added to the middle heap. Then, the upper heap is diminished by the quotient obtained from dividing the middle heap by 64. This shall be the uncorrected day-count (asphuṭa-dinagaṇa). Having placed that in two positions, one should divide one of them by seven [to find the weekday]. If the weekday of that day is not correct, [the calculation must be adjusted].
Then, one and so forth should be added to or subtracted from the first heap as required so that the weekday may be correct; thus the true day-count (*ahargaṇa*) is obtained.

For the sake of purifying Mars, one hundred and sixty-seven is added to the true day-count, and the quotient obtained by dividing by the number of days in Mars’s revolution—namely, 674—is to be discarded as a completed revolution of the zodiac. In the same way, for the others as well, the remainder is multiplied by the [relevant] asterism and divided by its own revolution days; the quotient obtained is the asterism situated above.

From the remainder of that [value], multiplied by sixty, the quotient obtained by dividing by the days of its own zodiacal sign (maṇḍala) gives the *ghaṭīs*; below that, as before, are the *pāṇīpala*s and so forth. This [result] beginning with the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) should be placed in two locations; in one place, nine and a half asterisms are to be subtracted.
Then, for the Sun, it should be understood as stated for Aries and Aśvinī;
for that which is situated in the specific [sign], the principles are eighteen *adrās* for the slow motion (*mandakārya*), which serve as the steps (*pada*).
In the slow motion (*mandakarma*), the corrections (*deyāni*) for the subsequent [periods] such as the asterisms and so forth are to be applied;
however, in the fast motion (*śīghrakarma*), having placed the corrected longitude of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn— purified by their own slow motion— in two places, [one should proceed].

One [unit] is subtracted from the solar longitude when it is devoid of *ravikā*; when the lunar date (*tithi*) has been added and not yet subtracted, one should perform the subtraction of three quarters and six asterisms (*nakṣatra*) according to the rule. Thereafter, the procedure beginning with "if [the result] is a debt, as stated for the sun," up to the end of the sequence, should be understood here.
In this swift calculation, wealth (*dhana*) is to be added in direct order (*krama*), and debt (*ṛṇa*) is to be subtracted in reverse order (*utkrama*).
One should purify that [remainder] as far as possible; having understood the remaining term that indicates the planetary movement (*grahacaraṇa*), it is to be subtracted.

By that very term from the *Kālacakrāvatāra*, one multiplies the remaining *nāḍīs* and divides by sixty; the quotient, together with a portion of that term, represents the accumulated movements (*caraṇas*) traversed by the planet according to the sign (*rāśi*) and movement in the first half [of the month]. However, in the second half, one discards the portion of that term obtained by division and [counts] the non-traversed movements together with the other portion of that term.
Elsewhere, for the purification of slow-moving [planetary] motion, these fourteen steps are to be added or subtracted:
14, 3, 2, 18, 10, 36, 11, 3, 11, 8, 3, 0, 24, 5, and 3; these are from the base of the auspicious [earth].
From the horizontal line: 10, 10, 9, 8, 6, 6, 1, 1, 3, 3, and 6.
The *randhra* (nine), *rudra* (eleven), and *nṛyoga* (twenty-seven) are the steps for the Guru in swift calculation;
from the square root of four times five, five, five, four, four, two, two, and zero, there are the steps for Śauri (Saturn): two, four, five, five, eight, three, and three—this is half a verse.

Likewise, having placed the slow-sun (mandasūrya) in two places, one should subtract it from both the movement of Mercury and the movement of Venus. Then, having performed the subsequent procedure— beginning with "of that which has been subtracted" and ending with "the untraversed degrees"— as stated for Mars, [the results] are to be added to or subtracted from the other slow-sun.
In this very way, the period of Mercury and the period of Venus occur for the king and the lord of the earth respectively.
From that [period], the periods for Mars are nine, six, eleven, seven, five, and from the Mūla [nakṣatra] onwards, twenty, twenty-eight, and thirty-four;
and for Mercury, they are three, two, and twice the number of twice-born [twelve].
From the Mūla nakṣatra, there are two, six, three, eight, six, and three [yāmas] for the defects of the two eyes and the lunar days.

"Randhra-randhra-guṇa-adri" (993) is the position of Venus for the swift motion (*śīghracara*). Thus ends the purification of the swift motion (*śīghrakarma*) for Mars and the other planets. For the slow motion (*mandakarma*), in order to purify Mercury, one should take the clear day-count (*sphuṭadivasagaṇa*), multiply it by one hundred, and subtract three thousand two hundred and seven (3207). Then, divide by the days of Mercury's revolution (584,467)—starting with "mountains, apertures, etc. (*śaila-randhra-ādi-nāśaiḥ*)—and so forth, up to "pāṇīpala" and so on; this should be performed as for Mars. This [calculation] beginning with the asterism (*nakṣatra*) and so on is stated as the movement (*cāra*) for the purpose of the swift motion.

Therefore, for that purpose, having established the sun's longitude (sūryabhoga) devoid of the *ravikā* correction in two places, one should subtract sixteen and a half lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) from the sun's longitude in one place. Then, having applied the rules for Aries and so forth as stated for the sun—ending with "according to the nature of debt or credit"—those [mansions] should be added to or subtracted from the other sun's longitude;
thus, in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakarman*), Mercury is purified.
The *Kālacakrāvatāra* states:

This other solar movement is called the slow operation (*mandakarma*), which has attained the nature of pure Mercury; for the sake of the fast operation (*śīghrakarma*), there are ten mountains (seven) and fire (three) steps in the slow work of the Sun.

For the sake of the purification of Jupiter (*guru*), one should perform the calculations as for Mars (*bhauma*), starting from the subtraction of the quotient obtained by dividing the clear day-count (*sphuṭāhagaṇa*)—diminished by 260—by the days in Jupiter’s cycle (364), and so forth.
Here, however, is the distinction: twelve lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are to be subtracted, and the steps (*pada*) are 913.

For the sake of the purification of Venus (*śukra*), one should perform everything as for Mercury (*budha*), starting from the subtraction of ten times eighty-four from the clear day-count, and then dividing by the days in Venus’s cycle (584), and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: six constellations (nakṣatras) are to be subtracted; the steps (padāni) are fifty-two (five arrows and two moons).

For the sake of purifying Saturn, from the count of clear days reduced by eighty-four (sky-eyes-eight-Vedas), one should perform the calculation starting with "the quotient obtained by division by sixty-six-one-hundred-thirty-three" and so forth, as in the case of Mars. The distinction, however, is that eighteen constellations are to be subtracted, and the steps are twenty-two (twenty-two lunar days and zeros).
Thus is the purification of Mercury and the other planets in their slow-motion (manda-karman).

Furthermore, the planetary position purified by the slow-motion operation becomes the same as that purified by the fast-motion (śīghra-karman) when purified by both operations; it is not the case that the planetary position purified by the slow-motion operation is one thing and the one purified by the fast-motion operation is another—so say those who know the scriptures.

The enjoyment (*bhoga*) is purified by two operations: for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, it is by the slow operation (*mandakarma*) alone; for the Sun, by the slow operation alone; and for the Moon, by the fast operation (*śīghrakarma*) alone. For the purpose of calculating Rāhu’s enjoyment of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), one should subtract from the pure months—increased by two and twelve—the portion obtained through the divisions of zero, six, seasons, and four oceans, using Rāhu’s fortnight-mandala (*pakṣamaṇḍala*). This subtraction is performed by doubling the months for the sake of the heap of fortnights (*pakṣarāśi*); adding one fortnight for the full moon for the sake of the lunar eclipse; and adding two fortnights for the new moon for the sake of the solar eclipse. The quotient thus obtained is to be discarded.
From the remaining degrees, for the purpose of the asterism (*ṛkṣa*), multiply by twenty-seven; the asterism obtained by dividing by ten thousand (10,000) is the result.
From the remainder, multiply by sixty; the ghaṭīs obtained by dividing by ten thousand are the result.
From that remainder as well, likewise [multiply by sixty], the liptās [are obtained].
The remainder of that, divided by six, gives the breaths (śvāsa) obtained from [the signs] beginning with Aries;
subtracting this obtained [value] from twenty-seven constellations results in the mouth-occupation (mukhabhoga) of Rāhu.
That same mouth-occupation, when mixed with thirteen and a half constellations, becomes the tail-occupation (pucchabhoga).

Thereafter, in the solar transit for each month, there is the descent of two constellations into the Kālacakra: eleven ghaṭikās per month; over six months, twelve constellations amount to sixty-six ghaṭikās;
and thus, thirteen [constellations] become fifty-three.
Here, in the solar transit, during a solar eclipse or the transit of the new moon (amāvāsyā), solar minutes (ravikā) are to be added or subtracted.
Then, having subtracted forty-five *ghaṭikās* from Rāhu’s [total] course (*bhoga*), one should subtract the remainder as the course of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
In that case, if the lunar mansion is equal [in extent] to either the mouth or the tail [of Rāhu], only then does an eclipse occur, and not otherwise.
Alternatively, having calculated the new moon day according to the previously mentioned method, one should subtract the solar course (*sūryabhoga*) from either Rāhu’s mouth-course or tail-course.

During a lunar eclipse on the full moon day, one should subtract the longitude of the Moon from the longitude of Rāhu’s mouth or from the longitude of his tail; if it is equal to the mouth or the tail in terms of the asterism (nakṣatra), an eclipse occurs.
Not otherwise.

For here, at the junction of the lunar nodes (*parvasandhi*)—either at the end of the new moon or the end of the full moon—the orbs of the sun and the moon enter the orb of Rāhu. The term "orb" (*maṇḍala*) should be understood as sixty *nāḍikās*, which is the passage through one asterism (*nakṣatra*); that [asterism] consists of twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and sixteen digits (*kalā*).
In that regard, if the passage of these two [the sun and moon] is subtracted from the passage of Rāhu, then there is a total eclipse lasting for the duration of sixty *nāḍikās*.
When half the [lunar] portion is pure, there is a half-bite.
As long as Rāhu has entered the fourth part of the digit (kalā), which consists of four nāḍīs, the conjunction of the planets is to be known.
And when Rāhu swallows [the moon] in the mouth-portion, then it is the eastern part.
And the tail and body [occupy] the western portion;
in this way, the other directional divisions are to be understood. The commentary states that "the turning [of the shadow] occurs elsewhere" and that "this happens in exactly six months.
In ultimate reality, Rāhu, whose nature is darkness, swallows the moon itself because of its cool rays.
It is not the sun;
rather, at the time of the end of the new moon (amāvāsyā), because the moon has entered the sun,
there is the conventional expression that "the sun swallows [the moon]."
Thus is the purification of Rāhu.

Ketu, having entered the solar disc, moves daily for four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *liptās*, which is the extent of the Sun's movement; it moves two and a half *liptās* further in its swift motion, proceeding forward in direct motion (*anuloma*) and backward in retrograde motion (*viloma*).
Having remained thus for three years, it emerges.
Having emerged, it rises for two *ghaṭīs* every day, and that *ghaṭī* consists of fifty-six *liptās*. For one month, Ketu is seen like a star, smokeless;
thereafter, for one fortnight, the smoke-bannered comet (*dhūmaketu*) becomes manifest.
Thus, at the end of one and a half months, she again becomes invisible for three years on the solar disc in the same manner.
Her initial rising should be understood by observing it according to common renown.
In this way, her rising is known once in the *Kālacakra-avatāra* as occurring after an infinite time; this is the purification of Ketu.
In this regard, the general rule is as follows:
when a planet has risen from the solar disc and moves forward in its swifter motion, its occupation of the first half of fourteen *caraṇa*-units of time is called "swifter course" (*śīghracāra*);
its occupation of the latter half is "slower course" (*mandacāra*).
Then, when half the circle has been relinquished, there is the departure from the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
It is said that in the first half there is the movement within the circle (*cakracāra*), while in the second half there is the exit (*nirgamagati*),
due to the abandonment of the circle of zodiac signs and lunar mansions.
In this sequence, in the first half there is an increase in wealth and the planets face the east;
in the second half there is a loss of wealth and they face the south.
In the reverse sequence, in the first half there is an increase in debt and they face the west.
In the latter half [of the month], there is a loss of debt for those facing north.

For these [planets], facing other directions occurs due to the influence of portents (*ariṣṭa*) and so forth; by nature, however, Rāhu faces west and circumambulates Meru clockwise, while the other planets face east.
Therefore, because it is covered by the rays of the sun, there is no total absence of the planet when the sun sets;

likewise, its rising occurs again here in this region due to the decrease and increase in the movement of the sun and moon, resulting in an increase of the day by the number of *nāḍīs* obtained as a tenth part of the sixty *nāḍīs* that constitute the nature of a day-and-night (*ahorātra*).

At night, there is a decrease [of the day]. From the boundary of the *dakṣiṇāgni* circle up to the boundary of the *mahāhimavat* circle, during the six months of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), there is an increase of seventy-five thousand *yojanas*.

In this way, from the time of the great solstice at the winter solstice until the solstice at the southern fire (the summer solstice), there is an increase in the night and a decrease in the day during the southern course of the sun.
This being so, it should be understood that for each successive day and night, there is a decrease or an increase of two *liptās*.

Likewise, from the lands of Bhoṭa, Līca, China, and so forth, up to the region of Sambhala, there is a decrease or increase of three *liptās* plus four breaths per day and night, calculated by dividing [the total] into nine, eight, or seven parts; in the Kailāśa section, it is six parts. Beyond the Kailāśa section toward the Himagiri mountain, there is a decrease or increase of three *liptās* plus four breaths per day and night. Outside the Himagiri, in the eight directions, there is a single sphere of the lunar mansions and zodiac signs in the form of a circle, with the equatorial line (*viṣuva-rekhā*) at its center.

Here, on both sides, it is bow-shaped; and here, in the middle of the threshing floor, the constellations beginning with Aśvinī revolve like a circle of intellect, a moon, or a bull, up to half of Citrā on the northern line.
On the southern side, however, [they revolve] from half of Citrā down to Revatī; in this same manner, two and a quarter constellations constitute one zodiac sign (*rāśi*).
Thus, there are twelve zodiac signs, and the planets are their consumers.
And of this globe, its northern limit proceeds from the northern fire-circle;
however, during the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), its southern limit touches the southern edge of the Snow Mountain (*Himādri*).
Regarding the descent of the Wheel of Time (*Kālacakra*): during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), it is at the southern limit.
The southern fire-circle and so forth move [toward the north];
the northern limit, however, touches the northern edge of the Snowy Mountain (Himavat).
And these constellations and so forth revolve clockwise around Sumeru by the power of their motion, forming a spherical shape.
The measurement of the globe extends from the circle of the Dakṣiṇāgni mountain to Mahāhimavanta for seventy-five thousand *yojanas*.
From these, the sun abandons each daily directional division obtained by dividing [the total] by one hundred and eighty-two and a half, which is the number of days in half a revolution.
Thus, the sun’s transverse movement across the twelve sectors should be understood; this is the method of calculation (*karaṇamārga*).
However, even so, there is never purity for the Sun by way of the process of calculation;
when the longitude of the Sun is thus impure, Mars and the other planets,
though corrected, do not become true, being like trees whose roots have perished.

Therefore, the established method is stated as follows: On level ground, one should draw a circle with a radius of one cubit (*hasta*). At its center, a gnomon (*śaṅku*) measuring two *vitastis* is placed. In the forenoon, as the shadow of the gnomon gradually contracts from the outside, when it enters the central point of the line on the circumference of the circle, a mark (*cihna*) or the sign of a crow’s footprint (*kākapada*) should be made at that spot; this very point is the western direction. In the afternoon, however, as the shadow gradually expands from the center of the circle, [the same procedure is followed] until it reaches the aforementioned point.

The previous mark should be made; that very [line] is the east and so forth here. Holding a thread over one mark, one should draw a circle with a small stick from the other mark toward the south. Then, holding a thread over the other mark, one should do likewise, so that it forms the shape of a fish.

In the middle of those two circles, the center of the fish's mouth faces south, and the center of its tail faces north; thus are the directions determined. Having erased those two circles, the examination should be performed at midday, beginning from the tenth day prior to the day of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).
There, from the center of the first mandala, the northern boundary line enters the center of the mandala;
on whichever day that is the day of the sun’s transit into the northern course (uttarāyaṇa),
on that day— with that weekday, that lunar date (tithi), that yoga, and that karaṇa— the solar transit begins with Vaiśākha and so forth.
The fundamental constant (*mūla-dhruvaka*) for the nine signs beginning with Aries over nine months is twenty *ghaṭikās* in the place of asterisms and fifteen in the place of *ghaṭikās*.
Therein, in that constant, one should subtract the solar degrees by adding four *daṇḍas* and twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s every day, which represents the descent of the Kālacakra.

By the previously mentioned procedure—beginning with "those three quarters and six lunar mansions are to be purified," and so forth—it is likewise stated in the *Mūlatantra*: "Starting from the solstice, [the correction] should be applied every day until another solstice occurs;
according to the prescribed ritual procedure, the solar position is to be purified."

And thus, the results of the days of the week, lunar dates, asterisms, yogas, karaṇas, zodiac signs, and planetary transits are easily understood from other sources; therefore, they are not elaborated upon here. This auspicious exposition of astrology has been proclaimed; may the wise man, having descended into this *Kālacakra* which brings about ultimate welfare, easily master its composition without hindrance. May the Great Sage forgive this work composed by me. May this path of discernment, which dispels the darkness of the heart, spread throughout the world. And may the merit of this [work] bear fruit as the wealth of the Jina throughout the three realms.
Thus ends the *Kālacakrāvatāra*.

Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces: [Planetary positions] 4, 1, 4, 1, 4, 6, 1, 3, 4, 6, 0; [Ghaṭīs] 17, 53, 22, 24, 51, 47, 16, 37, 04, 52.
